Physics × ML — ODE demos

Where neural networks meet differential equations

An illustrated tour, from planetary orbits to space weather.

Dipak Munshi  ·  26 September 2026  ·  every figure generated from scratch in pure JAX / NumPy / Matplotlib

A great deal of physics is written as ordinary differential equations — a rule for how something changes from one instant to the next. A planet's orbit, the slow exchange of a moon's eccentricity and tilt, the daily rise and fall of the ionosphere, the plunge of a geomagnetic storm: all are ODEs, and for a century we have solved them by integration, stepping the rule forward in time.

Machine learning does not replace that picture; it augments it in four specific places. A network can infer the parameters of an ODE from noisy data, emulate an expensive solve so it runs thousands of times faster, integrate the dynamics more stably when its architecture respects a conservation law, and forecast a driven system in real time. The five demos here are one clear example of each — and each manufactures its own data, so every result is reproducible from the code alone.

One caution runs through all of them, the same lesson as in radio-interference work: a network is trustworthy where you need speed, breadth or search, and least trustworthy when asked to guarantee something the physics promises — a conserved quantity, the honest width of a posterior — unless that guarantee is built in rather than hoped for.

Use the arrows below, the number buttons above, or your keyboard's ← → keys to move between pages.

Demo 1 · Planetary · Inference

Kozai–Lidov cycles: reading an orbit from a noisy record

Place a planet or moon on an orbit steeply inclined to a wider companion star, and its eccentricity and inclination trade places in a slow, periodic dance. As the orbit is torqued the eccentricity climbs — the body swings ever closer at pericentre — while the inclination falls. Throughout, one combination of the two is exactly conserved:

Θ = √(1 − e²)   cos i = constant

The inclination bottoms out near the famous 39.2° critical angle, a number that falls straight out of the equations.

The Kozai–Lidov cycle: eccentricity (blue) rises as inclination (grey) falls. Press play.

The mechanism drives the tilts of irregular satellites, the eccentricities of many exoplanets and the merging of compact binaries. The practical question is inverse: given only a noisy record of the eccentricity, can we recover the orbit's starting point? Here we do it exactly — for every candidate (e₀, i₀) we integrate the equations, compare to the data, and map the whole posterior on a grid, with a Gaussian ellipse laid over the top.

Left: the oscillation with noisy observations. Right: the exact posterior, recovering the truth (white ×) as a degenerate ridge, with 1σ and 2σ Gaussian ellipses.
Result
The true start (e₀, i₀) = (0.05, 65°) is recovered as a tight but curved, degenerate ridge: the parameters trade off along the conserved Θ, and the elongated ellipse is itself the warning that a single “±” would mislead.
Why it matters: the same inference machinery — and the same honesty about posterior width — underlies orbit recovery for satellite tracking and the trajectory-inference problems in radio interference.
Demo 2 · Planetary · Emulation

A neural surrogate for the ODE, far faster than integrating

Every inference in Demo 1 integrated the ODE once per trial — thousands of solves for a single posterior. Scale that to a survey, a nested-sampling run, or simulation-based inference over many datasets, and the integration becomes the wall you hit. This is where emulation earns its place: we train a small network to reproduce the map from orbit parameters straight to the observable, learning it once from a few thousand examples:

network:   (i₀, e₀)  ⟶  e(t)
Left: the emulator (red, dashed) against the true ODE (blue) on orbits it never saw. Right: a parity plot of every eccentricity in the test set.

Thereafter it never integrates anything — it evaluates a whole batch of orbits in one matrix multiplication. This is the pattern behind the fast orbital-stability classifiers that replaced billion-orbit N-body runs, the interior-structure emulators that invert planet compositions, and the neural retrievals now standard in exoplanet atmospheres.

Result
The surrogate reproduces the solver to an RMSE of 0.022 in eccentricity and runs tens of times faster than integrating (68runs 51× faster than integrating — 800 orbits in 0.6 ms against 30 mstimes; here) runs 51× faster than integrating — 800 orbits in 0.6 ms against 30 msmdash; a batch of 800 orbits in 0.46runs 51× faster than integrating — 800 orbits in 0.6 ms against 30 msnbsp;ms against 31runs 51× faster than integrating — 800 orbits in 0.6 ms against 30 msnbsp;ms. The advantage compounds with every call, so the win grows exactly where you can least afford the cost.
The catch: an emulator is only as good as the region it was trained on. Push it far outside and it extrapolates blindly — the failure the next demo cures with structure.
Demo 3 · Planetary · Structure-preserving

Symplectic versus plain networks: conserving energy

Suppose we learn the dynamics themselves: a network that, given the state of an orbit, returns how it changes. Have it output the rate of change directly and it works locally — but integrate forward for many periods and the orbit quietly spirals, because the learned field has no reason to conserve energy. The fix is to teach the network physics: a Hamiltonian network learns a single scalar — the energy H — and derives the motion from its symplectic gradient:

dq/dt = ∂H/∂p     dp/dt = − ∂H/∂q

Because any such flow conserves H by construction, energy cannot drift no matter how long you run it.

Left: the plain network (red) spirals off the Kepler orbit; the Hamiltonian network (blue) stays bound. Right: relative energy error against time, log scale.

Both networks are trained on identical data and fit the instantaneous motion equally well. The difference appears only in the long rollout — and it is stark.

Result
With the same data and solver, the plain network's energy drifts to a ~650% error while the Hamiltonian network holds at ~1%. Long-term stability came from structure — a built-in conservation law — not from more parameters.
Why it matters: this is why physics-informed and symplectic networks are taken seriously for long N-body integration and molecular dynamics, where a slowly leaking energy budget silently corrupts every downstream result.
Demo 4 · Space weather · Inference

The Chapman ionosphere: the Sun making and unmaking a plasma

High above us, the Sun's extreme-ultraviolet and X-ray photons strip electrons from the thin upper atmosphere, creating the ionosphere; left alone, that plasma recombines. The balance is one elegant production–loss equation:

dN/dt = q(t) − α N²

The production q(t) follows the Sun across the sky — strong at noon, absent at night — while the quadratic term is recombination. The result is the daily breathing of the ionosphere.

Left: solar production (yellow) drives the electron density (blue) up by day; recombination decays it at night. Right: the posterior over the two governing parameters.

The inverse problem is the one an ionospheric physicist faces: from a noisy density record, what are the two numbers that set the layer — peak production and recombination rate? As before, we map the full posterior exactly over (q₀, α).

Result
The parameters are recovered as a clean diagonal degeneracy: they are not separately pinned down, because the daytime plateau depends only on their ratio through N ∝ √(q₀/α). Breaking it needs the shape of the night-time decay — a physical insight the posterior hands you for free.
Close to home: this same electron density, integrated along the line of sight, is the total electron content that smears low-frequency radio interferometry — the very effect ionospheric calibration in the SKA era must remove.
Demo 5 · Space weather · Forecasting

Geomagnetic storms: a network that learns the Burton equation

When the solar wind arrives carrying a southward magnetic field, it couples to the magnetosphere, pumps energy into the ring current, and the Dst index plunges by hundreds of nanotesla before slowly recovering. The textbook model is the Burton equation:

dDst/dt = − k·VBs − Dst / τ

The first term is the drive set by the solar-wind coupling VBs; the second is the relaxation back to quiet on a timescale τ.

Top: the incoming solar-wind driver. Bottom: the true storm from the Burton equation (blue) and the neural forecast (red, dashed), rolled forward from the solar wind alone.

This is a genuine operational problem — power grids, satellites and navigation all care about the next few hours of Dst. We simulate hundreds of storms from random drivers, train a small network to predict the next Dst from the current state, then let it forecast a storm it has never seen, stepping forward using only that storm's solar wind.

Result
On a held-out −232 nT storm — a strong event — the network reproduces the whole main phase and recovery to an RMSE of 1.3 nT, driven only by the upstream solar wind. This is, in miniature, how operational Dst and total-electron-content nowcasts are built from ACE and DSCOVR data.
The honest footnote: a point forecast this good still says nothing about its own uncertainty — and in space weather, as in interference inference, the width of the prediction is often what the decision hinges on.
Demo 6 · Magnetohydrodynamics · Forecasting & chaos

The Rikitake dynamo: magnetic reversals and the horizon of prediction

Two conducting discs, each driving the other's magnetic field, make the simplest self-exciting MHD dynamo — a toy model of the churning liquid-iron core that generates Earth's magnetism. The fields (x, y) and the differential rotation z obey three coupled equations:

dx/dt = −μx + yz   •   dy/dt = −μy + x(z − A)   •   dz/dt = 1 − xy

For μ=1, A=5 the system is chaotic: the field wanders and flips sign at irregular intervals — exactly the aperiodic polarity reversals written into the palaeomagnetic record.

Left: the field reversing between normal (blue) and reversed (red) polarity — a toy geodynamo. Right: forecasts of the field from a fixed start, and where they diverge.

Now the twist that makes this the honest counterpoint to the storm forecast. A network learns the flow almost perfectly — its fit error is tiny. Yet rolled forward, the forecast tracks the true dynamo only for a while and then peels away; and so does a near-perfect physics model started from an initial condition off by just one part in a thousand. Both diverge, because the system is chaotic: errors grow exponentially, and prediction carries a built-in horizon set by the Lyapunov time.

Result
The neural forecast follows the true field for roughly 11 time units before chaos takes over; even the exact model with a 10−3 initial error is capped near 33. No amount of model quality removes that ceiling — it is a property of the physics, not the method.
The contrast with Demo 5: the geomagnetic storm was a driven, relaxing system and forecast beautifully; this dynamo is internally chaotic, so the very same tools hit a wall. Knowing which regime you are in is half the battle — and it is why long-range reversal and space-weather prediction are fundamentally hard.
Discussion

A small taxonomy

Read together, the five demos sort neural networks into four honest roles. Inference (Demos 1 and 4) turns noisy data into constrained parameters — and its recurring lesson is that the interesting structure lives in the degeneracies, the curved ridges where parameters trade off, which a single error bar cannot express. Emulation (Demo 2) buys speed by replacing an expensive solve with a learned surrogate, and pays for it only at the edges of the training set. Structure-preservation (Demo 3) shows that a network built to respect a conservation law earns a stability no amount of extra data confers. And forecasting (Demos 5 and 6) drives a learned model in real time — spectacular for a driven, relaxing storm, yet bounded by a hard predictability horizon the moment the system turns chaotic, as the dynamo shows.

The thread that ties them is one principle: a neural network is most valuable where you need speed, breadth or search, and most dangerous where it is quietly asked to guarantee something — energy, a calibrated width, a physical constraint — that only the physics can promise. The remedy is never “more parameters”; it is to fold the guarantee into the model, or to keep the exact calculation for the one quantity that must be exact. That is the same conclusion reached, from a very different direction, in the task taxonomy for artificial intelligence in radio-frequency interference.

All five demos run on pure JAX + NumPy + Matplotlib, each generating its own data — nothing loaded from disk.
